Medicine.question: ১) Which of the following is a 1st line antitubercular drug?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is ethambutol. Ethambutol is one of the first-line antitubercular drugs used in the standard treatment regimen for tuberculosis.

The commonly used first-line anti-TB drugs are:

  • Isoniazid (H)

  • Rifampicin (R)

  • Pyrazinamide (Z)

  • Ethambutol (E)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ethionamide – A second-line anti-TB drug, mainly used in drug-resistant tuberculosis.

  • Prothionamide – A second-line drug similar to ethionamide, used for multidrug-resistant TB.

  • Kanamycin – An injectable second-line aminoglycoside, used in resistant TB (less commonly used now due to toxicity).

High-yield points:

First-line TB drugs = HRZE

  • H → Isoniazid

  • R → Rifampicin

  • Z → Pyrazinamide

  • E → Ethambutol

Important adverse effects:

  • Isoniazid → Peripheral neuropathy, hepatitis

  • Rifampicin → Orange discoloration of body fluids, hepatotoxicity

  • Pyrazinamide → Hyperuricaemia, hepatotoxicity

  • Ethambutol → Optic neuritis (red-green colour blindness)

Medicine.question: ২) What is the minimum amount of pleural fluid requires to be clinically detected?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is 200 ml. Clinically detectable pleural effusion usually requires approximately 200–300 ml of pleural fluid. When this amount accumulates, physical signs such as stony dullness on percussion and reduced breath sounds may become detectable.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 100 ml – A small amount of pleural fluid may be detected by imaging (especially ultrasound), but it is usually not detectable clinically.

  • 300 ml – May produce clinical signs, but the commonly quoted minimum detectable amount clinically is around 200 ml.

  • 500 ml – A larger effusion; clinical signs are usually obvious at this volume.

High-yield points:

  • Pleural effusion:

    • Ultrasound can detect very small amounts (~10–50 ml)

    • CXR (PA view) usually detects around 200–300 ml

    • Clinical examination detects approximately 200 ml or more

  • Clinical features:

    • Stony dull percussion note

    • Reduced breath sounds

    • Reduced vocal resonance

    • Reduced chest expansion

Medicine.question: ৩) Which one is the most common organism of atypical pneumonia?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is Mycoplasma pneumoniae. It is the most common cause of atypical pneumonia, especially in young adults and school-aged children. It commonly causes a gradual onset of symptoms with dry cough, low-grade fever, and minimal chest findings compared with the severity of radiological changes.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Chlamydia – Can cause atypical pneumonia, especially in infants and older adults, but is less common than Mycoplasma.

  • Coxiella burnetii – Causes Q fever pneumonia; it is an uncommon cause of atypical pneumonia.

  • Influenza – Can cause viral pneumonia but is not classically considered the most common cause of atypical pneumonia.

High-yield points:

Atypical pneumonia common causes:

  • Mycoplasma pneumoniae (most common)

  • Chlamydophila pneumoniae

  • Legionella pneumophila

  • Coxiella burnetii

  • Respiratory viruses

Mycoplasma features:

  • No cell wall → resistant to β-lactam antibiotics

  • Dry cough

  • Bullous myringitis

  • Cold agglutinins may be positive

  • Treated with macrolides/tetracyclines

Medicine.question: ৪) All of the followings are cause of unilateral pleural effusion except?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is CCF (Congestive cardiac failure). Pleural effusion due to CCF is typically bilateral because it results from increased hydrostatic pressure in the systemic and pulmonary circulation. Although it can occasionally be unilateral (more commonly right-sided), a unilateral effusion should prompt evaluation for other causes.

The other options are common causes of unilateral pleural effusion:

  • Pneumonia – Causes a parapneumonic effusion, which is usually unilateral and associated with infection/inflammation.

  • TB – Commonly causes unilateral pleural effusion, especially in young adults, due to pleural involvement.

  • Bronchial carcinoma – Can cause unilateral pleural effusion due to pleural metastasis or lymphatic obstruction.

High-yield points:

Common causes of unilateral pleural effusion:

  • Tuberculosis

  • Pneumonia

  • Malignancy (e.g., bronchogenic carcinoma)

  • Pulmonary embolism

Bilateral pleural effusion:

  • CCF (most common)

  • Nephrotic syndrome

  • Liver cirrhosis

  • Renal failure

Medicine.question: ৫) Which is the most common organism of CAP?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is Streptococcus pneumoniae. It is the most common causative organism of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in adults. It commonly causes typical pneumonia with fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, and lobar consolidation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • S. aureus – Can cause pneumonia, especially after influenza infection, in intravenous drug users, or in hospital settings, but it is not the commonest cause of CAP.

  • N. pneumoniae – This is not a recognized common pathogen causing CAP. (Possibly a distractor; Chlamydophila pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia.)

  • N. meningitidis – Rarely causes pneumonia and is mainly associated with meningitis and meningococcaemia.

High-yield points:

Most common CAP organism → Streptococcus pneumoniae

Typical CAP organisms:

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae (commonest)

  • Haemophilus influenzae

  • Staphylococcus aureus

  • Gram-negative bacilli (in selected patients)

Atypical CAP organisms:

  • Mycoplasma pneumoniae

  • Chlamydophila pneumoniae

  • Legionella pneumophila

Medicine.question: ৬) Which is the common side effect of INH?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is peripheral neuropathy. Isoniazid (INH) commonly causes peripheral neuropathy due to pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency. INH interferes with pyridoxine metabolism, leading to nerve damage, especially in patients with risk factors such as diabetes, malnutrition, alcoholism, and pregnancy.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hepatitis – True, INH can cause hepatotoxicity, but peripheral neuropathy is the classic and commonly tested adverse effect.

  • Skin rash – May occur with INH but is less characteristic.

  • Optic neuritis – Classically associated with ethambutol, not INH.

High-yield points:

Anti-TB drug adverse effects:

  • Isoniazid (H) → Peripheral neuropathy, hepatitis

    • Prevent with pyridoxine (vitamin B6)

  • Rifampicin (R) → Orange discoloration of body fluids, hepatitis

  • Pyrazinamide (Z) → Hyperuricaemia, hepatitis

  • Ethambutol (E) → Optic neuritis, red-green colour blindness

Medicine.question: ৭) What is the nature of percussion note in pneumonia?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is dull. In pneumonia with lung consolidation, the alveoli become filled with inflammatory exudate, replacing air with fluid and cells. This increased tissue density produces a dull percussion note.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Resonant – Normal percussion note over healthy air-filled lung.

  • Woody dull – Classically described in some cases of large pleural effusion, especially dense fluid collections, but not typical of pneumonia.

  • Stony dull – Characteristic of pleural effusion, where fluid accumulates in the pleural space.

High-yield points:

  • Pneumonia (consolidation) → Dull percussion note

  • Pleural effusion → Stony dull percussion note

  • Pneumothorax/emphysema → Hyper-resonant percussion note

  • Consolidation signs:

    • Bronchial breathing

    • Increased vocal resonance

    • Dull percussion note

Medicine.question: ৮) Which of the following doesn't correspond to radiological finding of moderate pleural effusion?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is trachea pulled to the same side. In a moderate pleural effusion, accumulation of fluid causes mass effect, and a large effusion usually pushes the mediastinum and trachea to the opposite side, not towards the same side.

The other options are radiological features of pleural effusion:

  • Curvilinear line – True. The upper border of pleural fluid forms a meniscus sign, which appears as a curved upper margin.

  • Costophrenic angle obliteration – True. Fluid accumulation blunts the costophrenic angle, one of the earliest X-ray signs.

  • Cardiophrenic angle obliteration – True. Pleural fluid can obscure the cardiophrenic angle, especially with larger effusions.

High-yield points:

Pleural effusion X-ray findings:

  • Blunting of costophrenic angle

  • Meniscus sign (curvilinear upper border)

  • Homogeneous opacity

  • Mediastinal shift:

    • Large effusion → trachea shifted to opposite side

    • Collapse/fibrosis → trachea pulled to same side

Medicine.question: ৯) What is the commonest organism for hospital acquired pneumonia?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is Pseudomonas aeruginosa. In hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP), especially in patients with prolonged hospital stay, ICU admission, or mechanical ventilation, Pseudomonas is one of the most common and important causative organisms due to its multidrug resistance and ability to colonize hospital environments.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • S. aureus – A common cause of HAP, particularly MRSA, but overall not the classical single best answer in many exam contexts.

  • S. pneumoniae – The most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), not HAP.

  • H. influenzae – Can cause respiratory infections but is more commonly associated with CAP and COPD exacerbations.

High-yield points:

Common organisms of HAP:

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa

  • Staphylococcus aureus (especially MRSA)

  • Klebsiella pneumoniae

  • Acinetobacter species

  • Enterobacter species

CAP commonest organism → Streptococcus pneumoniae
HAP/VAP important organism → Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Medicine.question: ১০) What is the appearance of pleural fluid in pneumonia?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is turbid. In pneumonia, pleural effusion occurs due to inflammation and is called a parapneumonic effusion. The pleural fluid usually becomes turbid or cloudy due to the presence of inflammatory cells, proteins, and sometimes bacteria.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Serous – Typically seen in transudative effusions such as congestive heart failure or cirrhosis; it is usually clear and straw-coloured.

  • Mucoid – Not a typical description of pleural fluid in pneumonia.

  • Blood stained – May occur in malignancy, pulmonary embolism, or trauma; it is not the characteristic appearance of uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion.

High-yield points:

Pleural fluid appearance:

  • Clear/straw coloured → Transudate (e.g., CCF)

  • Turbid/purulent → Infection (parapneumonic effusion/empyema)

  • Blood stained → Malignancy, PE, trauma

  • Milky → Chylothorax

Pneumonia → Parapneumonic effusion → Exudative, turbid fluid

Medicine.question: ১১) Appearance of crepitation means which pathological stage of CAP?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is stage of congestion. In the early stage of lobar pneumonia, pulmonary capillaries become congested and alveolar oedema with inflammatory exudate develops. This fluid within the alveoli causes fine inspiratory crepitations (crepitus indux).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Stage of red hepatisation – The alveoli are filled with red blood cells, fibrin, and neutrophils, causing consolidation. Bronchial breathing is more characteristic than crepitations.

  • Stage of grey hepatisation – Red blood cells disintegrate, while fibrin and inflammatory cells remain within the alveoli.

  • Stage of resolution – Alveolar exudate is cleared by macrophages. Crepitations may reappear (crepitus redux) before disappearing completely.

High-yield points:

Lobar pneumonia stages:

  • Congestion → Alveolar oedema with inflammatory exudate → Crepitus indux (appearance of crepitations)

  • Red hepatisation → Consolidation with RBCs, fibrin, and neutrophils → Bronchial breathing

  • Grey hepatisation → Fibrin and macrophages (RBCs disintegrate)

  • Resolution → Clearance of alveolar exudate → Crepitus redux (reappearance of crepitations)

Medicine.question: ১২) Which antitubercular drug should never be given in any stage of pregnancy?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is streptomycin. It is an aminoglycoside that crosses the placenta and can cause fetal ototoxicity by damaging the developing eighth cranial (vestibulocochlear) nerve. This may result in permanent congenital sensorineural hearing loss. Therefore, streptomycin is contraindicated throughout pregnancy.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Rifampicin – Generally considered safe in pregnancy and is included in the standard treatment regimen, although vitamin K supplementation may be considered near delivery because of a small risk of neonatal bleeding.

  • Ethambutol – Considered safe during pregnancy at recommended doses, with no proven increase in fetal malformations.

  • Pyrazinamide – Recommended by most international guidelines and widely used in standard first-line treatment of tuberculosis during pregnancy.

High-yield points:

  • Streptomycin → Contraindicated in pregnancy → Fetal ototoxicity (CN VIII damage) → Congenital sensorineural deafness.

  • Standard first-line anti-TB drugs considered safe in pregnancy: Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Ethambutol, Pyrazinamide.

  • Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) should be given with isoniazid during pregnancy to reduce the risk of peripheral neuropathy.

  • Active tuberculosis should be treated during pregnancy, as untreated disease poses a greater risk to both the mother and fetus than appropriate therapy.

Medicine.question: ১৩) What is the characteristic of fever in pneumonia?
Medicine.option2: fever with evening rise of temperature
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is fever with chills and rigors. Pneumonia, especially bacterial pneumonia such as pneumococcal pneumonia, classically presents with acute onset of high-grade fever accompanied by chills and rigors. This reflects the body's systemic inflammatory response to bacterial infection.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fever with night sweats – More characteristic of tuberculosis, lymphoma, or chronic infections.

  • Fever with evening rise of temperature – Classically seen in tuberculosis rather than acute pneumonia.

  • Fever with muscle pain – More typical of viral infections, especially influenza and dengue, although mild myalgia may occur in pneumonia.

High-yield points:

  • Pneumonia → Acute high-grade fever with chills and rigors

  • Tuberculosis → Evening rise of temperature, night sweats, weight loss

  • Influenza → Fever with prominent myalgia and headache

  • Pneumococcal pneumonia → Fever, chills, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, and crepitations/bronchial breathing on examination

Medicine.question: ১৪) If large amount of fluid is aspirated at a time there may be......?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is pulmonary oedema. During thoracentesis, rapid removal of a large volume of pleural fluid (typically >1.5 L at one time) can lead to re-expansion pulmonary oedema. This occurs when a chronically collapsed lung re-expands rapidly, causing increased capillary permeability and leakage of fluid into the alveoli. Although uncommon, it is a potentially life-threatening complication.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pneumothorax – A recognized complication of thoracentesis due to accidental pleural puncture, but it is not specifically related to aspirating a large amount of fluid.

  • Hydrothorax – Refers to accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity and is not caused by removing excessive pleural fluid.

  • Air embolism – A very rare complication of thoracentesis, usually due to inadvertent entry of air into the pulmonary veins, and is not related to large-volume aspiration.

High-yield points:

  • Large-volume thoracentesis (>1–1.5 L) → Risk of re-expansion pulmonary oedema

  • Pneumothorax is the most common procedural complication of thoracentesis.

  • Re-expansion pulmonary oedema is more likely when the lung has been collapsed for several days.

  • To reduce risk, pleural fluid is usually removed gradually, and the patient should be monitored for symptoms during the procedure.

Medicine.question: ১৫) What is the commonest complication of pneumonia?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is parapneumonic effusion. It is the most common complication of pneumonia and occurs when inflammation extends from the lung parenchyma to the pleural space, leading to accumulation of pleural fluid. Most parapneumonic effusions are sterile (uncomplicated) and resolve with appropriate antibiotic therapy, although some may progress to empyema if infected.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Empyema – An important complication in which the pleural fluid becomes infected with pus, but it is less common than parapneumonic effusion.

  • Lobar collapse – May occur due to bronchial obstruction by mucus plugs but is not the commonest complication of pneumonia.

  • Lung abscess – Results from necrosis of lung tissue, usually caused by aspiration or highly virulent organisms, and is a relatively uncommon complication.

High-yield points:

  • Parapneumonic effusion → Most common complication of pneumonia.

  • Empyema → Infected parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage in addition to antibiotics.

  • Lung abscess → Localized suppurative necrosis with cavity formation.

  • Persistent fever despite antibiotics should raise suspicion for parapneumonic effusion or empyema.

Medicine.question: ১৬) Which of the following is not characteristic of pleural fluid study in pleural effusion due to bronchial carcinoma?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is ADA level raised. Adenosine deaminase (ADA) is typically elevated in tuberculous pleural effusion because of increased T-lymphocyte activity. In pleural effusion due to bronchial carcinoma, the ADA level is usually normal or only mildly elevated, making a raised ADA level not characteristic.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hemorrhagic appearance – Malignant pleural effusions are commonly blood-stained (hemorrhagic) due to tumor invasion of the pleura.

  • AFB not found – Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) are usually absent in malignant pleural effusions.

  • Malignant cells may be found – Pleural fluid cytology may reveal malignant cells, helping to confirm the diagnosis.

High-yield points:

  • Malignant pleural effusion → Often hemorrhagic, exudative, and may contain malignant cells.

  • ADA >40 U/L strongly suggests tuberculous pleural effusion, especially in high-prevalence areas.

  • AFB smear is usually negative in both tuberculous and malignant pleural effusions due to its low sensitivity.

  • Pleural fluid cytology is the most useful initial test for diagnosing malignant pleural effusion.

Medicine.question: ১৭) Haemoptysis associated with fever, night sweats, weight loss is typical presentation for--?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB). The combination of haemoptysis, fever, night sweats, and weight loss is the classic presentation of active pulmonary tuberculosis. These constitutional symptoms reflect a chronic granulomatous infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Haemoptysis occurs due to erosion of blood vessels within cavitary lesions or inflamed lung tissue.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Bronchial carcinoma – May present with haemoptysis and weight loss, but fever and night sweats are not typical presenting features.

  • Pneumonia – Usually presents with acute fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, and chills, rather than chronic night sweats and weight loss.

  • Bronchiectasis – Characterized by chronic productive cough with large volumes of purulent sputum and recurrent infections. Haemoptysis may occur, but night sweats and weight loss are not typical features.

High-yield points:

  • PTB → Haemoptysis + fever + night sweats + weight loss (classic presentation)

  • Bronchial carcinoma → Haemoptysis, persistent cough, weight loss, smoker

  • Pneumonia → Acute fever, chills, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain

  • Bronchiectasis → Chronic productive cough with copious purulent sputum, recurrent infections, haemoptysis may occur

Medicine.question: ১৮) Continuation phase for relapse case of Tuberculosis is…?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is 5 months. In the previously treated (relapse) tuberculosis regimen (Category II), the continuation phase lasts 5 months and consists of Isoniazid (H), Rifampicin (R), and Ethambutol (E) after an intensive phase of 3 months.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 4 months – This is the continuation phase for new drug-susceptible TB cases in the traditional 6-month regimen.

  • 6 months – Not the standard continuation phase for the conventional relapse (Category II) regimen.

  • 8 months – Refers to the total duration of the older relapse treatment regimen, not the continuation phase.

High-yield points:

  • New TB case (traditional regimen) → 2 months intensive + 4 months continuation (2HRZE/4HR)

  • Relapse/previously treated TB (older Category II regimen) → 3 months intensive + 5 months continuation (2HRZES/1HRZE/5HRE)

  • Continuation phase of the older relapse regimen = 5 months

  • Note: Current WHO guidelines no longer recommend the Category II regimen. Relapse cases should undergo drug susceptibility testing (DST) and receive treatment based on the resistance profile. However, in many examinations, the expected answer remains 5 months based on the traditional regimen.

Medicine.question: ১৯) Non pulmonary complication of pulmonary TB excludes…?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is aspergilloma. It is a pulmonary complication of tuberculosis that develops when Aspergillus colonizes a pre-existing post-tuberculous lung cavity, forming a fungal ball. Therefore, it is not a non-pulmonary complication of pulmonary TB.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Empyema necessitans – Extension of tuberculous empyema through the chest wall into adjacent soft tissues; considered an extrapulmonary extension of TB.

  • Laryngitis – Results from spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the larynx, an extrapulmonary site.

  • Amyloidosis – A systemic complication of long-standing chronic tuberculosis due to secondary (AA) amyloidosis.

High-yield points:

  • Aspergilloma → Colonization of a post-TB cavity by Aspergillus → Pulmonary complication

  • Tuberculous laryngitis → Extrapulmonary spread to the larynx

  • Empyema necessitans → Extension of tuberculous empyema through the chest wall

  • Secondary (AA) amyloidosis → Late systemic complication of chronic tuberculosis

Medicine.question: ২০) Which is not true about viral pneumonia?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is normal CXR finding. Although chest X-ray findings in viral pneumonia may be less dramatic than in bacterial pneumonia, the chest X-ray is usually abnormal, showing bilateral diffuse or interstitial infiltrates. Therefore, a normal chest X-ray is not a characteristic feature of viral pneumonia.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Abrupt onset – Viral pneumonia often presents with an acute onset, particularly with influenza.

  • Dry cough – A dry, non-productive cough is a typical feature of viral pneumonia.

  • Leucopenia – Leucopenia is commonly seen in viral infections, including viral pneumonia.

High-yield points:

  • Viral pneumonia → Acute onset, dry cough, fever, myalgia

  • CXR → Usually shows bilateral interstitial or diffuse infiltrates, not a normal finding

  • Leucopenia is more suggestive of viral than bacterial infection

  • Bacterial pneumonia → Productive cough, neutrophilic leukocytosis, lobar consolidation on CXR
